Many thanks,
Lucy

messages.body_plain:
Good morning Lucy.

Could you provide us with more information on this? What version of the  Distance and  mrds packages are you using that generated the warning? Did you recently update these packages (CRAN update about three weeks ago)?

Let me understand the biological scenario. You have a model that incorporates vegetation strata (as a factor covariate I presume) in the detection function. However, you have detections for which there is no record of the vegetation strata, correct?  How many detections do you have? How many vegetation strata? How many detections per vegetation strata?

The software might provide you with an AIC score, but it might be the case that the estimates are not maximum likelihood estimates if convergence was not achieved. Have a look at the estimated covariate coefficients and more importantly their standard errors to see if they appear to be unusually large. Those would be the steps I would follow if I saw this warning.

I suspect there is insufficient support in your data to fit this model; i.e. some strata may have few detections. Without seeing your data, that's just a guess. In such situations, you might collapse the strata into fewer levels or not model the effect of the vegetation covariate as pooling robustness ensures unbiased estimates of abundance even when failing to include features that might affect detectability.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I am an undergrad student working on a project measuring the species-specific relationships between bird populations and bark beetle caused tree mortality in a wilderness area of Colorado. I have a fairly large dataset of 160 points in which distance sampled point counts were conducted over this past summer along with several field-collected and remotely sensed covariates corresponding to each point (and observation in the dataset). So far, I have had generally good success working through the analysis using the Distance package in R, but have continually encountered the following error when using the "formula=" argument in data subsetted for different species to model relationships with the other covariates: "Error in checkdata(data, region_table, sample_table, obs_table, formula) :Variable(s): obsRCKI are in the model formula but not in the data." This is just an example, but I continually get the same error in all other covariates (ndviclass, ndvi, temp, wind, elevation, timecategory, mortalityseverity, etc.) being modeled, and for all other species-subsetted datasets. I do not however get the error in the non-subsetted dataset (see screenshot) or when the analysis is run without any covariates in the subsetted data (see screenshot). I have ensured there are no missing values anywhere in the subsetted datasets, and have checked the data types to ensure numeric values are in fact numeric (as.numeric function) and character values are read as such (as.character function).

I have also ensured that I am using the most current version of R, RStudio, and the Distance package for the analysis. I have included screenshots of my dataset, my code for subsetting the data and subsequent attempts for analysis at the species level. To rule out errors in subsetting, I have also attempted exporting the subsetted data to a csv, checking it over in Excel, and re-importing it with the code using the newly imported csv - same error. Potentially this is an easy fix as I am only in my first few months of using the distance package, but have spent substantial time attempting to resolve it with no luck so far. Any help or suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks so much,
Arrow Myers
Western Colorado University

Welcome to the list and thanks for your question and supporting screen shots.

messages.subject: DSM and "weights" argument
messages.body_plain:
Good afternoon wonderful distance sampling group,

I am creating a dsm with line transect data for a species of alpine songbird. These data were collected in extremely rugged terrain and the line transects are not straight lines within an alpine basin, they follow the curvature of the basin, sampling across a habitat suitability gradient, so "good", "marginal", and "bad" habitat are all represented. Because some assumptions are relaxed using a dsm (like non-randomly placed lines) we decided to use this modeling method, as well as wanting to draw ecological inference about a species with little available information.
I am curious about the "weights" argument that can be included in the dsm modeling. Because of the rugged alpine terrain, transects are not uniform in size, shape, and area. So I have a column in my "segdata" data frame (with information about line transect segments) that is the area surveyed for each line transect segment.
My questions are these:
1. How is the "weights" argument used in the dsm (when not specified in the model). It seems from the dsm R Documentation page (?dsm) that when weights is not included in the model, it is set to weights = NULL, which would assume that all line transect segments were the same length and covered the same area. Is that correct? Or does the model calculate the surveyed area (as 2 * truncation distance * Effort (line segment length) from the "segdata" dataframe?
2. In what context is it appropriate to use the "weights" argument and specify the actual surveyed area of the line transect segment? I wasn't sure if this is an appropriate argument to include if I'm using "count" as the response. May I use the "weights" argument with my area column (from segdata) specified with the "count" as response or is it only appropriate to use with "abundance.est" as the response?
3. When I did include the weights=segdata$segment.area call in my dsm (with count as the response), my deviance explained went from 36% (no weights argument) to 56.5% (weights argument specified), and all variables were suddenly extremely significant (all p-value = <2e-16), whereas in the model without weights  the p-values had a wide range of values (from 0.049 to <2e-16). Why would the deviance explained shoot up so drastically and p-values all drop to <2e-16?
*Obviously, if it is inappropriate to use "weights" in the count as response model, I don't need to worry about this, I just need to remove the term.
4. I am also not clear when it is appropriate to use "count" as the response vs. "abundance.est" vs. "density.est" for response variable. My detection function did not improve by including covariates, and from what I have read I could use either "count" or "abundance.est", but I am not clear on when or why I would use the different model responses. Also, do I need to format the input data in the "segdata" file differently for each of these response types?

Thank you for your time and energy answering these questions or providing articles or other scholarly materials for me to review.
Warm regards,
Kat Bernier
PhD candidate
University of California, Santa Cruz

Dear distance-sampling list,

I am very pleased to announce new software, training and web site releases from CREEM:

Distance for Windows 8.0

This new version of our Windows-based software is distributed with a new msi installer, which removes difficulties associated with installing the software under the latest versions of Microsoft Windows. We have also included the latest versions of the distance sampling R packages for those using the R-based analysis engines.  We recommend users of Distance for Windows download the new version, available at https://distancesampling.org

Free online training

We have created a completely new version of our free online course “Introduction to Distance Sampling”.  Content has been refreshed, lectures re-recorded and exercises updated.  We have added a new chapter on mark-recapture distance sampling.  The new course is available at https://distancesampling.org/online-course. This easy-to-navigate course website is structured to explore distance sampling concepts from fundamental through double observer methods for estimating detectability on the transect. It is searchable so concepts can be accessed easily to serve as a refresher.

In addition to this free course, we continue to offer periodic online interactive training workshops – details of current offerings are at  https://distancesampling.org/training/training.html.

New web portal

We have refreshed and updated our web site https://distancesampling.org.  The new site works better on a variety of screen types.  We have created a separate landing page for each of our R libraries (mrds, Distance, dssd, dsims and dsm), accessible by selecting Software, R-packages.  These searchable pages contain an online manual for the package was well as a set of articles giving case studies (“vignettes”) on software usage.  These case studies are also accessible from the main distancesampling.org <http://distancesampling.org> page by selecting Resources, Case studies. Each case study has tags to categorise it so users can search by category, rather than needing to know the case study they seek.

New R package versions

As previously announced, we have recently released new versions of our mrds (3.0.0) and Distance (2.0.0) R packages.  These feature an improved optimization engine for conventional distance sampling.  They can be downloaded from CRAN.

These developments have been funded by the UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) via an Impact Acceleration Account grant to the University of St Andrews.  We are grateful for their support.

We hope you find these improvements useful in your distance sampling endeavours.  Please get in touch with any comments or suggestions. We encourage you to pass along these web addresses to others who either use distance sampling or are new to the subject.

Best wishes,

Len Thomas and the Distance development team

messages.body_plain:
Eric

Welcome to the list.

The summaries of fitted model objects produce only two measures of precision in estimates of detection probability: standard error and coefficient of variation. If you want a third measure of precision, namely confidence intervals, you'll need to calculate those yourself.

Here is a bit of code that performs the confidence interval computation based upon the assumption the confidence interval is approximately log-normally distributed (Sect 6.2.1 of Buckland et al (2015):

library(Distance)
data("wren_snapshot")
cu <- convert_units("meter", NULL, "hectare")
easy <- ds(wren_snapshot, key="hr", transect = "point", convert_units = cu)
out <- summary(easy$ddf)
# extract P_a and se from summary object
P_a <- out$average.p
P_a_se <- out$average.p.se <http://average.p.se>[1,1]
P_a_cv <- P_a_se / P_a
# assume degrees of freedom >30
zed <- 1.96
# use log-normal based confidence intervals
C <- exp(zed*sqrt(log(1+P_a_cv^2)))
ucb.log <- P_a * C
lcb.log <- P_a / C
print(paste("CI bounds for P_a", round(lcb.log,4), round(ucb.log,4)))

If you have questions, let me know.
